subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: Stealth: Engineering Invisibility
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Stealth: Engineering Invisibility.

hook.text: The F-117 Nighthawk looked like no other aircraft. Its flat angular surfaces weren't for aerodynamics — they were for radar.

buildup.text: Radar bounces radio waves off surfaces. A round fuselage reflects signals back to the source. Flat angles deflect them away.

discovery.text: Radar-absorbing materials coat the surface, turning radio energy into heat. Shape and coating together minimize radar return.

twist.text: The F-117 was so aerodynamically unstable that it needed computers to fly. Without fly-by-wire, it would crash instantly.

climax.text: The B-2 Spirit improved stealth with curves instead of facets. Modern computers can calculate radar returns from smooth shapes.

punchline.text: Hide from radar. Sacrifice aerodynamics. Let the computer fly.

quiz.question: Why did the F-117 require fly-by-wire computer control?
options: The cockpit was sealed for stealth, so pilots couldn't see outside
Its angular stealth shape was aerodynamically unstable without computer assistance
Radar-absorbing materials made the control surfaces too heavy to move manually
